articles.title: Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi
articles.summary: Pups that carry your shopping are one thing – but what about the mechanical canines being bought up in the US by ICE? Or the mutant mutts due to be developed by a startup called Warhound? Have you ever wanted to hang out with a dog with no fur, no face and a chip in its shoulder?
body: What exactly will these machines do when they can act more independently? The founder of Dimensional insists they will help people. They might carry groceries home, for example, which is certainly something my tiny chihuahua-mix is incapable of.

While it is nice to think that robo dogs are all going to be very good boys, there is a darker side to the industry. A couple of months ago it was reported that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) planned to spend up to $2m (£1.5m) on robot dogs made by the company Boston Dynamics. ICE has said the dogs won’t be used for anything nefarious but, considering everything the agency has been up to lately, this isn’t particularly reassuring.

articles.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: eye creams that are worth using down to the last drop
articles.summary: Face cream is often enough, but if you want a separate product for your eyes, these new ones are terrific value. A hill I will die on: you do not necessarily need an eye cream. There are, I will admit, reasons why you might fare better with one.
body: It may, of course, be none of the above, but just that you find using an eye cream a pleasure, which is as good a reason as any.

My point is that eye creams are not the anti-ageing magic bullet that marketing campaigns would have us believe. Very many of us can do the same job with our facial skincare, saving time and cash. But if you would still like to try one without the considerable financial commitment that many require, there are some new eye creams that represent terrific value for money.

The Inkey List has a number of eye creams at great prices that cleverly address most of the variables above. Its latest offering, Bio-Active Ceramide Eye Cream (£15), is ideal for someone who prefers a fresh, watery day cream but craves a little richness around the eyes. It provides lasting, creamy, expensive-feeling hydration without feeling greasy, and it absorbs quickly. A peptide complex may support an improvement in firmness long-term (the company says a three-month blind clinical trial yielded positive results).

articles.title: ‘Every family has silences’: Kathryn Hunter on despair, desire, dislodgeable limbs – and her acting genius
articles.summary: She has played King Lear, all three witches in Macbeth and an ape turned variety performer in Kafka’s Monkey. As she prepares for a new show, she discusses the soaring highs and deep lows of her extraordinary life. Kathryn Hunter pulls off her black beanie and sits down.
body: She is working on a stage adaptation of Eurotrash, Christian Kracht’s novel about a mother, played by Hunter, who is accompanied on the final trip of her life by her son, played by Ben Whishaw. As the pair come to terms with their dark past – and Europe’s – they must confront what Hunter describes as a “hinterland of silence”. In this case, it stems from the family’s Nazi ties, but Hunter believes “people will relate to it … in that every family has silences”. Working on the play has got her thinking about her own mother – and about the actor Marcello Magni, the co-founder of Complicité theatre and the love of Hunter’s life, who died in 2022 at 63.

Four years ago, Hunter ended her own long silence by clarifying that the life-changing injuries she suffered at 23 were not the result of a car accident, as was widely reported, but a suicide attempt. It was a sort of “coming out”, she says: “To come clean and make the plea for people in trouble to reach out and break silence … and rediscover the miracle that life can be.” She wants others to know that suicidal feelings “can be healed and it’s not something to be ashamed of; anyone can fall through the loop”.

articles.title: ‘A true icon of the hair industry’: celebrity hairstylist John Frieda dies aged 75
articles.summary: Businessman styled stars such as Twiggy, Madonna and Joanna Lumley and created popular hair care line Frizz Ease. John Frieda, the celebrity hairstylist who launched his own bestselling hair product range, has died aged 75.
body: In an Instagram post, his salon wrote: “It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully … surrounded by his family.
“John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.

“His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us. We will continue to do him proud. Our thoughts are with John’s family and everyone who loved him. Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts.”

The London-born businessman, whose father was a hairdresser and whose grandfather was a barber, styled celebrities ranging from Twiggy and Jackie Kennedy Onassis to Scarlett Johansson, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Diana, Princess of Wales.

articles.title: What to Read, Watch, and Listen to According to the Spring 2027 Collections
articles.summary: Designers dished on their inspos, we listened and collated their cultural touchstones of the season to help you get inspired. Here are all the movies, books, and music,that influenced the spring 2027 collections.
body: Our extensive analyses of the spring 2027 season now contine into the broader realm of culture. This, on the heels of decoding the trends —both what to where and how, clocking the art influences, and highlighting trenchant quotes from the reviews.

One way to fill in the six-month lag between the close of the season and the arrival of clothes in stores is to go deeper into designers’ inspirations. The list below collects the books, movies, and tracks that inspired the spring 2027 collections.

“The astounding Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève played host to Alessandro Michele’s latest Valentino show. For the occasion, Michele produced a sort of bibliography of imagined books, complete with descriptions, made-up authors, and phony ISBNs. Among the many creative titles were A Garden of Small Errors, Elsewhere Is a Precise Place, and The Social Life of Velvet. In the copious show notes, he talked up the value of an ‘anti-library’ of unread books (a concept lifted from the Lebanese American scholar Nassim Nicholas Taleb), comparing the enormous potential such a trove contains to a closetful of unworn clothes.

articles.title: Forget Arrakis, Zendaya’s Latest Look Comes From a London Auto Shop
articles.summary: If Ronan McKenzie called her latest collection “Going Places,” it did just that when Law Roach enlisted the designer to dress Zendaya.
body: Earlier this week, Zendaya appeared alongside her co-star Timothée Chalamet in a promotional video for Dune: Part Three, wearing look three from the show: a sleeveless halter-neck top and barrel-legged trousers in sandy shades of suede evocative of the movie’s desert landscape.

It’s always a thrill to see how far a collection can travel beyond the runway, particularly when it comes from a label with relatively modest resources. This was only McKenzie’s second runway presentation since joining the London Fashion Week schedule, staged in a mechanic’s garage and modeled by the designer’s inner circle, among them her mum, British Vogue contributing editor Zezi Ifore and entrepreneur Charlene Prempeh.

“Their presence underscored a central idea behind the collection: these clothes are intended to live beyond the runway,” read the show notes. “Going Places is grounded in pieces that can move through different bodies, ages, and lives.” Another headline-making moment from Selasi’s recent runways was the rediscovery of 59-year-old model Evelyn Effrim-Botchey, who has since gone on to make waves on Paris’s most rarefied catwalks.

articles.title: A '90s Prada Obsessive Picks Her Four Favorite Collections
articles.summary: Laia Garcia-Furtado, author of "Prada in the Nineties" shares her four favorite Prada collections.
body: Even as a devotee, the research process yielded a treasure trove of information about Mrs. Prada, like the fact that the designer’s spring 1999 collection was actually her way of fighting back against the trends of the ’90s (trends, of course, she helped popularize). “The spring 1999 collection with mirror embellishments was her sort of ‘taking the piss’ to the hippie trend that was happening around the time,” says Garcia-Furtado. “I love when you see her humor peeking through, and that really reminded me of the lace collection from fall 2008 —another one of my all-time favorites—that she said she made because she hated lace.”

Because the book is unauthorized and unapproved by Prada—as she wittily notes on her cover—Garcia-Furtado tapped illustrator Rachel Song to reimagine her favorite collections (think a chinoiserie look on page 133 or the spring 1999 bumbag on page 167). When asked if she’s sent a copy to Prada headquarters yet, she had a pithy reply: “You can’t just reach out to God like that.” Here’s to hoping a copy makes its way to Milan regardless.

articles.title: How to Sing Karaoke Every Night, in Every Borough of New York City
articles.summary: Two writers spend a week singing their way through karaoke bars across New York, exploring nightlife’s most vulnerable third space.
body: A more rigorous history might question whether Inoue really invented the first such machine or whether that credit belongs to electronics manufacturer Shigeichi Negishi’s Sparko Box a decade earlier. But the meteoric takeoff of karaoke has soared far past its humble—and slightly murky—origins. A portmanteau of the Japanese words kara, meaning empty, and oke, meaning orchestra, karaoke evokes both loneliness and collective belonging. Nearly 60 years on, we still root for the little machine that could—and all the brave singers who bare their heart through age-revealing ballads and club classics.

Perhaps nowhere is karaoke’s full breadth more on display than in New York City, where, on one side, you’ve got lounges complete with floor-to-ceiling video walls and speakers with built-in auto-tune capabilities and, on the other, decades-old dives whose performers are as much an institution as the establishment.

articles.title: The Specific Pain of Outgrowing an Adult Friendship
articles.summary: “It would be easy to say that these friendships had tumultuous endings with clean breaks, where the lines of right and wrong were clearly drawn,” writes Chanté Joseph. “But they weren’t, which makes it even more painful.”
body: The specific experience of grieving a friendship break-up that cannot be located in a single event is a form of “frozen grief,” a term coined by psychologist Pauline Boss. You are frozen when you cannot process such a loss because its cause is unclear.

What I lacked in clarity consumed me with sadness. Kat Vellos, author of We Should Get Together and founder of community program Platonic Action Lab, describes friendship as blooming from four seeds of connection: proximity, frequency, compatibility, and commitment. When the end of a friendship cannot be traced to a single moment of betrayal, she says, it can often be attributed to the absence of one of these seeds.

articles.title: Why the Algerian Sahara Should Be Your Next Off-Grid Adventure
articles.summary: Once one of the most closed-off nations in the world, Algeria is beckoning travelers at last. The vast Sahara offers an unforgettable introduction.
body: I woke up in the small hours of the night. Orion’s Belt was directly above where I lay on a thin roll-up mattress, zipped into a canvas sleeping bag. The hunter’s three luminous studs stood out in a canopy awash with stars from horizon to horizon, the Milky Way a glittery paint stroke across the scene. Aside from an occasional shuffle or snuffle from my fellow campers, the night was draped in a thick blanket of stress-shrinking quiet. It’d been days since I had cell reception. I could practically hear my nervous system thanking me.

You don’t need to sleep al fresco while camping in the Sahara Desert—I could crawl back inside my own pop-up dome tent at any time—but I’d certainly recommend it. It was a highlight of my trip to Algeria’s tranche of this continent-spanning desert.

I was in the Sahara on a nine-day tour with Explore Worldwide, a UK-based small-group tour company, which began running trips to Algeria earlier this year, partly as a reaction to the country’s new, albeit cautious, encouragement of tourism. I wanted to find out what that development looked like on the ground and experience the desert region that hopes to attract new visitors.

articles.title: There's a New Luxury Sleeper Train Route Coming to the French Riviera Next Spring
articles.summary: The legendary Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, a Belmond train, will travel from Paris to Monaco for the first time in 2027, with an overnight journey along the Côte d'Azur.
body: As someone who travels a lot for work, I would give anything to swap a flight for a train —even if that means spending eight hours on the rails.

Thankfully, it's easy to travel Europe by train at nearly any price point. And although I am a big fan of modern high-speed routes, the most romantic way to see the continent is certainly aboard one of Belmond's gorgeous luxury trains, which travel to destinations such as the British countryside, the Amalfi Coast, and the Scottish Highlands.
But in 2027, my bucket-list Belmond journey is a glamorous new addition to its already impressive collection of itineraries: the French Riviera.
The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express offers three cabin types: Historic Cabins, Suites, and Grand Suites.
